SEC27A-01.note: Two independent clauses (grower moved...; a sheltered block...flowered) need a semicolon. Comma tempts by reading 'a sheltered block...' as an appositive to 'orchard', which leaves 'flowered' subjectless; colon is weak since clause 2 does not explain clause 1.

SEC27A-02.note: Head noun 'milk' is singular and the present 'comes back' sets present tense: 'is kept'. 'was kept' lures via past 'injected'; 'were/are' lure via 'quarter'/'cows'.

SEC27A-03.note: Elliptical clause stands for 'rarely have trouble sprouting'; a main-verb 'have' is replaced by do-support in American English, and 'samples' is plural: 'rarely do'. 'rarely have' is the strong distractor (British-style main-verb have ellipsis), not standard here.

SEC27A-04.note: 'A booster...turned out to raise...' is a new independent clause, so a period. Comma tempts as an appositive to 'dose' but strands 'turned out'; colon joins a clause that does not elaborate the first.

SEC27A-05.note: Plural 'probes' plus duration 'for nine growing seasons' require present perfect progressive 'have been measuring'; 'has' lures via 'estate', 'are measuring' ignores the duration.

SEC27A-06.note: Compound subject (veterinarian and technicians) takes 'have'; 'their' pairs with the plural birds/subject. Pronoun antecedent is somewhat loose ('their' best reads as the birds of sentence 1; 'its' has no singular antecedent with antibody levels).

SEC27A-07.note: 'Certain species' (no article) is plural, and present 'is not planted' sets present: 'are holding'. Attractors 'marigold'/'row' pull to singular; 'were' lures via past 'sowed'.

SEC27A-08.note: 'the hand-rub bottles...were used' is a noun-clause object of 'found'; no punctuation between a verb and its object. Semicolon leaves 'When...the auditors' a fragment.

SEC27A-09.note: Ellipsis of 'is dependable' mirroring the main clause's 'are...dependable'; singular 'program' gives 'usually is'. 'usually does' is the strong distractor for those who treat the gap as a main verb.

SEC27A-10.note: Possessive needed before 'graft'; 'the final join of a long career' identifies one propagator, so singular 'propagator's'. 'propagators'' lures via the plural 'propagators' in sentence 1.

SEC27B-01.note: Restrictive participle: only the specimens from the blue-ice edge, contrasted with those from the interior, so no punctuation. Comma and a sentence-final single dash would both make it nonrestrictive (all specimens), which the contrast rules out; period leaves a fragment.

SEC27B-02.note: Plural 'readings'; 'long-demolished' landing stage sets past: 'were taken'. 'was taken' lures via 'pier'; 'are taken' via present 'hold'.

SEC27B-03.note: 'marks the first time that' (present main clause) takes present perfect; singular 'bank': 'has been superseded'. 'was superseded' is common colloquially and is the strongest distractor; 'have' lures via 'bays'. Slight defensibility risk for C.

SEC27B-04.note: Verb is far away: 'has always...subsided'; singular 'level'. 'is always' fails because 'subside' is intransitive and cannot be passive.

SEC27B-05.note: An earthquake has one epicenter, so the participial phrase is nonrestrictive: comma. No-comma A is the strongest distractor (reduced relative); colon before a participial phrase is nonstandard; period leaves a fragment.

SEC27B-06.note: 'dish' takes 'is'; the agents are the motors (plural, from 'No motor working alone'), so 'them'. 'it' lures to dish/frame.

SEC27B-07.note: Singular 'drive'; 'made obsolete by the light's automation' sets past: 'was being cranked'. 'were/are' lure via 'prisms'; 'is' via present 'records'.

SEC27B-08.note: Garden path: 'overflow surges' is a plural noun phrase, not subject+verb, so 'have carved'; present 'sits' supports perfect over 'were carving'. 'has carved' lures via 'overflow'/'spillway'.

SEC27B-09.note: Plural 'wires', past narrative ('wedged'), predicate adjective 'brittle' needs a linking verb: 'were also'. 'have also' fails because no participle follows.

SEC27B-10.convention: A single dash may introduce a sentence-final identifying element; 'ship—Kittiwake Star, a trawler...' is grammatical with the comma setting off a nested appositive
SEC27B-10.note: Name follows title noun with no punctuation; D splits the name, C is a fragment. A is defensible because the dash element runs to the sentence end and needs no closing mark; also the passage makes the ship unique, which strictly favors a nonrestrictive mark.

SEC27C-01.note: Comma ends the introductory clause after intransitive 'played', so 'the pipes...' is the main subject. B and C read 'the pipes' as the object of 'played', leaving 'often sounded' without a subject; colon after a dependent clause is never right.

SEC27C-02.note: Singular 'portrait', present 'crowd' (whenever...): 'is damp'. Attractors 'donors''/'frescoes'; 'was' lures via 'began admitting last spring'.

SEC27C-03.note: Plural 'bronzes' plus 'since the museum opened' require present perfect: 'have been displayed'. 'has' lures via 'temple'/'collector's'.

SEC27C-04.note: 'then a second mask...' continues the object phrase (in the mask of a king, then a second mask): comma. Semicolon tempts as if 'then' were a conjunctive adverb but leaves a fragment; colon and no punctuation are wrong.

SEC27C-05.note: Plural 'copies' takes 'follow'; the object is the singular 'psalter' (exemplar): 'it'. 'follows' lures via 'psalter'.

SEC27C-06.note: Singular 'helper', past 'caught fire': 'was splicing'. Attractors 'projectionists''/'archives keep'.

SEC27C-07.note: Plural 'tracks'; a specific past time ('on the night of the closing concert') excludes present perfect: 'were performed'. 'have been' lures via 'have circulated...since'.

SEC27C-08.note: Compound subject (the warden...and his clerk) is plural, and 'recording' needs progressive 'are': 'seldom are'. Minor risk: 'chosen by the members and his clerk' could be parsed as a single subject, making 'seldom is' arguable, but 'his clerk' choosing the warden is implausible.

SEC27C-09.note: 'the sheet' is the object of 'proofread'; the comma closes the introductory clause before subject 'pressmen'. A misplaces it ('the sheet pressmen'); B runs object and subject together; semicolon after a dependent clause is wrong.

SEC27C-10.note: 'chart' is the main verb ('the historians chart corrections...'); possessive options turn 'chart corrections' into a noun phrase and leave no verb; singular 'historian' disagrees with 'chart'.

SEC27D-01.note: Colon after a complete clause introduces the list that specifies the households. A comma appositive list is the strongest distractor but blurs into the series; B makes the relative clause ungrammatical ('reached homes'); semicolon leaves a fragment.

SEC27D-03.note: Plural 'cashiers'; 'in the paper-ticket years' (now over) excludes present perfect: 'were logging'.

SEC27D-04.note: Ellipsis of 'have crept upward too' mirroring 'has crept'; plural 'hours': 'have too'. 'has too' lures via 'outlet'/'highway'; 'are too' misreads the ellipsis.

SEC27D-05.note: Phrasal verb 'ruled out' takes 'raising...' as its direct object; no punctuation between verb and object.

SEC27D-06.note: Singular 'registrar' takes 'was'; the object is the singular questionnaire: 'it'. 'them' lures via 'answers'; 'were' via plural near nouns.

SEC27D-07.note: Singular 'turnout'; 'that autumn' sets simple past: 'was typical'. 'were' lures via 'renters'/'blocks'; 'has been' ignores the dated time.

SEC27D-08.note: Ellipsis of 'borrows' (present main verb) needs do-support; singular 'teacher': 'often does'. 'do' lures via 'dialects'.

SEC27D-09.note: Colon after a complete clause introduces the specification of where. A and C garble 'least outlying'; semicolon leaves a fragment.

SEC27D-10.note: Possessive before 'tally'; the last sentence ('the contractor who had written the lower figure') shows several contractors wrote it, so plural 'contractors''. Singular 'contractor's' is the strong distractor if the final sentence is not read.

tells: Verb+pronoun 2x2 grids: the key's verb number and pronoun number differ (crossed pairing) in SEC27B-06, SEC27C-05, SEC27D-06; only SEC27A-06 is a matched pair. A test-taker who learns 'pick the crossed cell' gets 3 of 4.

Agreement items routinely place the nearest noun with the opposite number to the key (SEC27B-02, SEC27B-03, SEC27B-07, SEC27B-08, SEC27C-02, SEC27C-03, SEC27D-02, SEC27D-04, SEC27D-08); 'pick against the adjacent noun' is a heuristic that works more often than chance, though it is close to the rule itself.

Tense-number 2x2 items: present perfect is the key only when a duration/since phrase appears (SEC27A-05, SEC27C-03) and loses whenever a dated past phrase appears (SEC27C-07, SEC27D-03, SEC27D-07); consistent with the rule, not a tell beyond it.
No mark-type tell found in punctuation items: keys spread over semicolon, period, comma, colon and none.
near_duplicates: new independent clause after a noun with a tempting appositive reading
elliptical auxiliary choosing do versus be versus have
introductory dependent clause comma placement around a possible object
colon before a specifying list or phrase after a complete clause
possessive number decided by context later in the passage
verb number crossed with pronoun number grid
no punctuation between a verb and its object
tense plus number grid with a time cue elsewhere
